subtopic: Being left out of a party
passage:
'Why are you sitting in the dark?' Gautam flicked on the light.
Sonali wiped her face fast. 'No reason.'
'Sonu.' He sat on the bed. 'What happened?'
'Mitali had a birthday party on Saturday. At the bowling place. Everyone went. Everyone. They were showing photos today, and I didn't even know.'
Gautam whistled softly. 'Ouch.'
'Was it because I'm boring? Or my clothes?'
'Maybe her mother said only twelve kids. Maybe she forgot. It doesn't mean you're boring.' He nudged her. 'It still stinks, though.'
'It really stinks.' She laughed a little, wetly.
'Want to go and get kulfi? My treat. And tell Mummy at dinner, she'll want to know.'
Sonali grabbed her slippers. 'Pista kulfi.'
'Obviously.'

qa.q: Where was Mitali's birthday party?
qa.a: At the bowling place.

qa.q: What was Sonali worried about as she sat in the dark?
qa.a: She felt hurt and left out, worried she was excluded for being boring or because of her clothes.

qa.q: What helped Sonali with the hurt?
qa.a: Talking to Gautam, hearing other possible reasons like numbers, and doing something nice for herself, a kulfi outing 🙂

qa.q: How does Gautam see the missing invitation?
qa.a: As painful but probably not about Sonali; he suggests a limit on numbers or forgetting.

grounding: A girl hurt at being left out of a classmate's party talks to her brother, considers other reasons, and does something nice for herself.

subtopic: Being left out of a party
passage: Last year, on a Monday, I found out that Mohit had invited the whole class to his birthday party at his uncle's farm. Everyone except me. I'm Devika. I heard it at the water tank, when two classmates were laughing about the hay ride. My ears rang. I spent the rest of the day pretending to read. At home I told Nani, and I cried properly. Nani didn't say 'forget it'. She said, 'That hurts. Let's make your favourite besan laddoos anyway.' So we did, and I licked the spoon. A week later Mohit told me, awkwardly, that his mother had used last year's class list, from before I joined. I still felt a small sting. But it wasn't about me.

qa.q: Where did Devika hear about the party?
qa.a: At the water tank.

qa.q: How did Devika feel on hearing about the party?
qa.a: Hurt and shut out; Devika's ears rang, and the rest of the day went on pretending to read.

qa.q: What did Devika do that helped?
qa.a: Told Nani and cried properly, then made favourite besan laddoos with her.

qa.q: How might Mohit have felt explaining about the class list?
qa.a: Awkward and embarrassed, realising Devika had been left out by mistake.

grounding: A child left out of a class party lets the hurt be felt, tells a grandparent, and later learns it was about an old list, not them.

passage: Food wasn't allowed in the computer lab at Himani's school in Noida. But she had been starving, and she'd sneaked in a carton of mango juice. Now there was a sticky orange puddle across keyboard seven. Her stomach dropped to her shoes. Dhruv, at the next computer, whispered, 'Wipe it and say nothing. Sir will never know.' She wiped it with her hanky. The keys still stuck. Himani imagined Sir finding it tomorrow and asking the whole class, and herself lying to his face. That felt even worse. When Sir came back, she stood up, knees shaking. 'Sir, I spilled juice on keyboard seven. I brought it in. I'm sorry.' Sir sighed. 'Thank you for telling me now. Bring a cloth, and no food in here again.'

qa.q: Which keyboard did the juice spill on?
qa.a: Keyboard seven.

qa.q: Why did Himani's stomach drop?
qa.a: She was scared of Sir finding out that she had broken the rule and damaged the keyboard.

qa.q: Why was owning up right away the better choice?
qa.a: It cost only a cloth and a warning, instead of the worse feeling of lying when Sir found it later.

qa.q: How might Sir have felt when Himani stood up?
qa.a: Annoyed about the keyboard but grateful for her honesty; he thanked her for telling him.

grounding: A girl frightened after breaking a lab rule is tempted to hide it, but owns up at once and gets off lightly.

passage:
'Parveen, why are you so pale?' Neelam whispered at recess.
Parveen pulled her closer. 'I took Ammi's phone to school. For photos on sports day. It's in my bag.'
'Phones aren't allowed! Ma'am checks bags on Fridays.'
'I know! My stomach's been flipping since assembly.' Parveen twisted her dupatta. 'I could hide it in the toilet cistern till home time.'
'And if someone finds it there? Then it's worse. You'd have to lie.'
'So what, I just give it to her?'
'Before the check. Tell her you brought it and you're sorry. Get it over with.'
Parveen swallowed. 'You'll come with me?'
'Obviously.'
Ma'am listened, locked the phone in her drawer and said, 'You can collect it at home time. Thank you for coming to me first.'

qa.q: On which day does Ma'am check bags?
qa.a: On Fridays.

qa.q: What was Parveen feeling since assembly?
qa.a: Scared and anxious about being caught; her stomach had been flipping.

qa.q: What did Neelam advise, and why was it wise?
qa.a: Hand the phone in before the check and apologise, because hiding it could lead to lying and bigger trouble.

qa.q: How did Ma'am respond to Parveen coming first?
qa.a: Calmly; she kept the phone until home time and thanked Parveen for coming to her first.

grounding: A girl scared after bringing a phone to school against the rules owns up before being caught, with a friend's support.

passage: 'Avni, you've been moping for three days about what happened at school. Let your Preeti Maasi tell you about the week I carried a stone in my stomach. I was ten. We weren't allowed on the school roof, but I climbed up for our ball and cracked two tiles. Nobody saw. That night I kept replaying the crack. The next day, and the next, it got heavier. I couldn't taste my food. I sat alone at recess, feeling like the worst girl in the world. On the fifth day I went to Sister Agnes. "I broke the tiles. I'm sorry." She had me help the gardener stack the new tiles and sweep up the old ones. After that, the stone was gone. Sitting with it alone didn't fix anything. Saying sorry did.'

qa.q: How many tiles did young Preeti crack?
qa.a: Two tiles.

qa.q: How did young Preeti feel in the days before she confessed?
qa.a: Heavy with guilt, as if carrying a stone; she couldn't taste her food and felt like the worst girl in the world.

qa.q: Which choice in the story finally lifted the guilt?
qa.a: Going to Sister Agnes, admitting it, saying sorry and helping to set things right.

qa.q: How might Sister Agnes have seen Preeti's confession?
qa.a: As honest and brave, deserving a fair way to make amends rather than a harsh punishment.

grounding: An aunt recalls days of heavy guilt after breaking a school rule, lifted only when she said sorry and helped fix it.

passage: It was the last day before the Diwali holidays, and Sumit had a horseshoe magnet hidden in his pencil box. He had taken it from the science lab on Tuesday, though borrowing without permission was strictly against the rules. Every day since, he'd felt it there like a hot coal. Now there were forty minutes till the bell, and the lab would be locked for two weeks. 'Just keep it,' Jatin muttered. 'Who'll notice?' Sumit pictured two weeks of holidays with the magnet in his drawer, thinking about it every night. No. He ran down the corridor to the lab. 'Sir, I took this on Tuesday without asking. I'm sorry.' Sir raised his eyebrows, then took it. 'Next time, ask. I'd probably have said yes.' Sumit ran for the bus, light as a kite.

qa.q: What did Sumit hide in his pencil box?
qa.a: A horseshoe magnet.

qa.q: What was Sumit feeling while the magnet sat in his pencil box?
qa.a: Guilty and uneasy, as if a hot coal were in there.

qa.q: Why was returning it before the bell the better choice?
qa.a: It let him say sorry and fix it now, instead of carrying the guilt alone all holidays.

qa.q: How did Sir react to Sumit's confession?
qa.a: Surprised but calm; he took it back and said he would probably have said yes if asked.

grounding: Just before the holidays a boy weighed down by guilt returns what he took and says sorry, instead of carrying it for weeks.

passage:
Monday. A new rule went up on the notice board: no football on the front lawn at lunch. Kunal kicked the wall. 'That's the silliest rule ever,' he told Lalremsiami. 'Sir just hates fun.' He wanted to play there anyway.
Tuesday. Kunal almost sneaked a ball out. Lalremsiami said, 'Why not just ask why?' He scowled, but it stuck in his head.
Wednesday. Kunal knocked on the sports teacher's door. 'Sir, why can't we play on the front lawn?' Sir showed him the window of the Class 1 room, cracked the week before. 'The little ones sit right there.' Kunal thought. 'What if we play on the back ground instead, and one of us looks after the ball bag?' Sir smiled. 'Write that down. I'll take it to the principal.'

qa.q: What did the new rule say?
qa.a: No football on the front lawn at lunch.

qa.q: What was Kunal feeling on Monday?
qa.a: Angry and resentful; he kicked the wall and thought Sir just hated fun.

qa.q: What did Kunal do on Wednesday that worked better than breaking the rule?
qa.a: He asked why the rule existed and politely suggested the back ground instead.

qa.q: How did the sports teacher see Kunal's question?
qa.a: Positively; he explained the reason, smiled at the idea and offered to take it to the principal.

grounding: Over three days a boy angry at a rule chooses to ask why it exists and suggest a change instead of breaking it.

passage: 'Ishita, you're furious about the no-coloured-clips rule? Let your Ankita Mausi confess something. At your age, our school made every girl wear two oiled plaits with black ribbons. I thought it was ridiculous. So I quietly started coming with one ponytail and hiding in the back row. For a month I was so angry at Mrs Fernandes I couldn't even look at her. Then she caught me, I got detention, and I was angrier still. My father asked, "Did you ever ask her why?" I hadn't. So I did. She said it was because of lice season, after half the class caught them. Then I wrote a polite letter asking if ponytails could be allowed outside lice season. The next year, they were.'

qa.q: What did young Ankita start coming to school with?
qa.a: One ponytail.

qa.q: What was young Ankita feeling toward Mrs Fernandes that month?
qa.a: Angry and resentful, so much that she couldn't even look at her.

qa.q: What choice in the story worked better than sneaking?
qa.a: Asking why the rule existed and writing a polite letter suggesting a change.

qa.q: How might Mrs Fernandes have felt when Ankita asked why?
qa.a: Probably pleased to explain, and open enough to consider the polite letter.

grounding: An aunt recalls quietly breaking a school rule she resented, and how asking why and suggesting a change worked better.

passage: 'Ankita, you're scared to tell Ma'am you lost the class register? Let your Ishita Bua tell you what happened to me. In Class 5, I was in charge of the class goldfish for the holidays. I forgot to feed it for four days, and it died. I thought my teacher, Mr Pinto, would shout the roof down. I almost lied and said it was sick. Instead, on the first day back, I stood at his desk and told him everything, crying. He didn't shout. He sat me down and said, "Thank you for being honest. What do you think we should do now?" We made a feeding chart together for the next fish. My whole body felt light. And after that, he trusted me with the class keys.'

qa.q: How many days did young Ishita forget to feed the goldfish?
qa.a: Four days.

qa.q: How did young Ishita feel when Mr Pinto didn't shout?
qa.a: Relieved; her whole body felt light after telling the truth.

qa.q: What choice in the story earned young Ishita trust?
qa.a: Telling Mr Pinto the truth instead of saying the fish was sick.

qa.q: How did Mr Pinto see Ishita's honesty?
qa.a: As something to thank and build on; he helped make a feeding chart and later trusted her with the class keys.

grounding: An aunt recalls admitting a mistake to a teacher who stayed calm and planned next steps, and how honesty earned trust.

passage: Twenty minutes into the maths exam, Nikita reached into her pocket for her eraser and felt a folded paper. Her revision notes, formulas and all, forgotten there since the bus. Her heart hammered. If anyone saw, they'd think she was cheating. The hall was silent except for the ceiling fans. She could shove it deeper and say nothing. Instead she raised her hand. Asif Sir came over, and she whispered, 'Sir, I just found my notes in my pocket. I didn't use them. I'm sorry.' She held them out. Asif Sir looked at her face, then took the paper calmly. 'Thank you for telling me. I'll keep it here. Carry on.' Nikita breathed out and went back to question six. Her hands stopped shaking by question eight.

qa.q: What was Nikita reaching for when she found the paper?
qa.a: Her eraser.

qa.q: What was Nikita feeling when Asif Sir took the notes calmly?
qa.a: Relieved; she breathed out, and her hands stopped shaking by question eight.

qa.q: Why was raising her hand the wise choice?
qa.a: Admitting it at once showed honesty and cleared any suspicion before it could grow.

qa.q: How might Asif Sir see Nikita after she came forward?
qa.a: As trustworthy; he stayed calm, thanked her and let her carry on.

grounding: In an exam hall a girl admits a mistake at once, the teacher stays calm, and she feels relieved and trusted.

passage: Behind the government school in their village near Nashik, the pond was strictly out of bounds. At recess Pankaj kicked the school football there anyway, waded in after it, and lost it in the weeds. Now Masterji was asking the class, 'Who had the ball?' Pankaj stared at Asif, begging with his eyes. Asif could say they'd played by the well. It would be easy. His chest tightened. After class, he pulled Pankaj behind the water tank. 'I won't lie for you. But if you tell Masterji, I'll come and stand with you.' Pankaj kicked the dust. 'I'll have to clean the classroom.' 'Then I'll help clean.' They went together. Masterji listened and gave Pankaj a week of sweeping. Asif swept beside him every day.

qa.q: What did Pankaj lose in the pond weeds?
qa.a: The school football.

qa.q: Why did Asif's chest tighten?
qa.a: He felt torn between loyalty to Pankaj and not wanting to lie to Masterji.

qa.q: How did Asif show real loyalty?
qa.a: He refused to lie but urged Pankaj to own up, went with him, and helped with the sweeping.

qa.q: What was Pankaj feeling when he stared at Asif?
qa.a: Scared of being caught and hoping Asif would cover for him.

grounding: A village boy refuses to lie for a friend who broke a rule, urges him to own up and stands beside him.

passage: At their school in Toronto, someone had drawn a cartoon rocket on the new bathroom door in permanent marker. The principal announced that whoever did it had until the end of the day to come forward. Dalia knew it was Bao. She had seen the marker in his hand. At lunch he said, 'You're my best friend. Just say you didn't see anything, okay?' Dalia's stomach knotted. She loved Bao's rockets. She didn't want him in trouble. But lying would drag her in too, and it wouldn't feel like friendship. 'I won't lie,' she said slowly. 'I think you should tell. I'll go with you, and I'll help scrub it off.' Bao groaned, then nodded. They went to the office together and spent Friday afternoon scrubbing, laughing at the stubborn tail flame.

qa.q: What was drawn on the bathroom door?
qa.a: A cartoon rocket.

qa.q: Why did Dalia's stomach knot when Bao asked her to lie?
qa.a: She felt torn: she cared about Bao and didn't want him in trouble, but lying felt wrong.

qa.q: What did Dalia offer instead of covering for Bao?
qa.a: To go with him to the office and help scrub the door, urging him to own up.

qa.q: How might Bao have felt walking to the office with Dalia?
qa.a: Nervous, but less alone and supported because she stood beside him.

grounding: A girl refuses to lie for her friend who broke a school rule, urges him to own up and helps him make it right.

passage: Sharmila had never once been late, never forgotten her ID card, never talked in assembly. So when Zeenat rushed into assembly at their Chennai school five minutes late again, Sharmila rolled her eyes and whispered loudly, 'Some people just don't care.' A few girls giggled. Zeenat flushed. At lunch, Sharmila sat at her usual table, and nobody joined her. She heard someone say, 'Miss Perfect.' It stung. Later she saw Zeenat at the gate, helping her little brother with his torn school bag. Maybe that was why she was always late. The next morning Sharmila didn't roll her eyes. At break she said, 'Is it your brother's bag again? I pass his class on my way. I can drop him at his line, if that helps you be on time.' Zeenat blinked, then smiled.

qa.q: How many minutes late was Zeenat to assembly?
qa.a: Five minutes.

qa.q: What did Sharmila feel when someone called her 'Miss Perfect'?
qa.a: Stung and lonely, sitting at her table with nobody joining her.

qa.q: How did Sharmila combine kindness with her respect for rules?
qa.a: Instead of scorning Zeenat, she offered to drop Zeenat's brother at his line so Zeenat could be on time.

qa.q: How might Zeenat have felt when Sharmila whispered 'Some people just don't care'?
qa.a: Embarrassed and judged; she flushed in front of everyone.

grounding: A girl who looks down on a late classmate finds scorn leaves her lonely, and offers kind help while still valuing rules.

passage:
'Ma'am, Arun's chewing gum. And Nisha's shoes aren't polished.' Tushar sat back, satisfied.
At break Damini caught up with him by the tap. 'Why do you do that?'
'Do what? Rules are rules.'
'You don't just tell. You smirk. Like we're dirt.'
'Well, I never break them.'
'Great. And nobody sits with you.'
Tushar opened his mouth, then shut it. It was true. Even his bench partner had moved.
'I'm not saying break rules,' Damini went on. 'Gum's not allowed. Fine. But you could just say, "Arun, bin it before Ma'am sees." Not make it a show.'
'That's... still following the rule.'
'Yes. Just not being horrible about it.'
The next day, Tushar leaned over. 'Arun. Gum. Bin it.' Arun blinked, and did.

qa.q: What was Arun doing that Tushar reported?
qa.a: Chewing gum.

qa.q: What was Tushar feeling when Damini said nobody sits with him?
qa.a: Stung and quietly embarrassed; he knew it was true, since even his bench partner had moved.

qa.q: What did Damini suggest instead of reporting with a smirk?
qa.a: Quietly telling Arun to bin the gum before Ma'am sees, keeping the rule without scorn.

qa.q: How do classmates like Damini see Tushar's reporting?
qa.a: As smug and unkind, as if he treats them like dirt.

grounding: A boy who scorns rule-breakers learns from a classmate that he can keep rules firmly without contempt.

passage:
Monday night
Diary, Siddharth here. Today Ma'am gave me the class monitor badge! I wore it all day. When she left for the staff meeting, I stood at the front and wrote TALKERS on the board, and everyone went quiet just because of me. It felt grand. Then Aparna, my best friend, started chatting with the girl behind her. I didn't write her name. But I wrote Raju's, for whispering less than she did. Raju saw. He looked at me like I was a cheat. My face got hot. When Ma'am came back, I told her, 'I missed one name,' and added Aparna's. Aparna sulked. But the badge is for being fair, not for bossing. Tomorrow I'm going to try harder.

qa.q: What did Siddharth write on the board?
qa.a: TALKERS.

qa.q: How did Siddharth feel standing at the front?
qa.a: Proud and grand, enjoying that everyone went quiet.

qa.q: How did Siddharth fix the unfairness?
qa.a: By telling Ma'am a name was missed and adding Aparna's, treating a best friend the same as everyone else.

qa.q: How might Raju have felt when his name went up but Aparna's didn't?
qa.a: Angry and cheated, since he had whispered less than she did.

grounding: A new class monitor enjoys the power, notices favouring a friend, and chooses fairness.

passage: In the village school near Hoshangabad, Jatin had been made monitor of the mid-day meal line. He walked up and down with his arms folded, like the sarpanch at the fair, and felt at least two feet taller. Then his cousin Ganga slipped in near the front, right beside the rice pot. 'Let me stay, na. We're family.' Behind her, a small girl from Class 1, who had been waiting since the bell, looked up at Jatin with big eyes. Jatin felt the job suddenly grow heavy. 'Ganga, back of the line,' he said. 'Same as everyone.' She glared and stomped off. Jatin's face went hot, but he kept the line moving and made sure the little girl got her plate first. Being monitor wasn't a prize, he realised. It was a job.

qa.q: What was Jatin the monitor of?
qa.a: The mid-day meal line.

qa.q: How did Jatin feel walking up and down with his arms folded?
qa.a: Proud and important, at least two feet taller.

qa.q: What made Jatin a fair monitor?
qa.a: He sent his own cousin to the back like everyone else, treating family and strangers the same.

qa.q: How might Ganga have felt being sent back?
qa.a: Annoyed and embarrassed, since she expected family to get special treatment.

grounding: A village boy proud of being a monitor treats his own cousin the same as everyone, seeing the role as a duty.

passage:
Monday. Behind the school, Eshaan and three other boys were daring each other to climb the old water-tank ladder, which had a rusted rung. Rehana watched one boy slip and grab the rail. Her heart jumped. She went straight to the PT teacher, who came running and stopped them. The ladder was chained that same afternoon.
Wednesday. 'Tale-bearer,' Eshaan hissed as Rehana passed. By lunch half the class was calling her that. Nobody passed her the ball. She ate alone, throat tight.
Thursday. Rehana told her class teacher, Mrs Iyer, about the name-calling. Mrs Iyer said, 'You may have stopped someone breaking an arm. That was right.' She spoke to the class that afternoon, and after school she phoned Rehana's mother. Rehana still felt sore. But she didn't feel wrong.

qa.q: What was wrong with the water-tank ladder?
qa.a: It had a rusted rung.

qa.q: How did Rehana feel eating alone on Wednesday?
qa.a: Hurt and left out; her throat was tight after being called a tale-bearer.

qa.q: What did Rehana do when the name-calling started?
qa.a: She told her class teacher, who backed her, spoke to the class and phoned her mother.

qa.q: Why might Eshaan be angry at Rehana?
qa.a: He may feel embarrassed at being stopped and blames her instead of seeing the danger.

grounding: Over several days a girl reports a dangerous dare, is called a tale-bearer, and gets support from a trusted teacher.

passage: 'Kavitha, they're calling you a snitch because you told? Listen to your Aditi Perimma. When I was eleven, two older girls were taking the little ones' tiffin boxes behind the toilets every day. One small girl was crying from hunger in class. I told our headmistress. The older girls were stopped that very day. But then my own class started calling me "tale-bearer". For a week nobody would sit with me. I cried on the way home. My mother went with me to the headmistress again, and she told the class, firmly, that telling about someone getting hurt is not tale-bearing, it's protecting. It still stung for a while. But that small girl brought me a guava every Monday for the rest of the year.'

qa.q: What were the older girls taking?
qa.a: The little ones' tiffin boxes.

qa.q: How did young Aditi feel during the week nobody sat with her?
qa.a: Hurt and lonely; she cried on the way home.

qa.q: What choice in the story helped Aditi during the name-calling?
qa.a: Telling her mother, who went with her to the headmistress so the class heard why telling was right.

qa.q: How did the small girl see what Aditi did?
qa.a: As protection and kindness; she brought Aditi a guava every Monday for the rest of the year.

grounding: An aunt recalls being called a tale-bearer for reporting harm to younger children, and how trusted adults backed her.

passage:
'Chaitanya! You broke the class globe?' Chandrika Ma'am's voice rang out.
'I didn't! It was already...'
'Enough. Outside.'
In the corridor, Chaitanya's chest burned. He wanted to kick the door and shout that she never listens.
At home, he slammed his bag down. 'Akka, she didn't even let me talk.'
His sister looked up from her books. 'You're angry. Fair enough. What will you say tomorrow?'
'That she's unfair!'
'Will that help?'
He breathed. 'No. I'll say it was cracked when I picked it up. Veena saw.'
Next morning he waited by the staffroom. 'Ma'am, can I say what happened yesterday? The globe was already cracked. I picked it up to show you. You can ask Veena.'
Chandrika Ma'am paused. 'Let's ask her.'

qa.q: What was Chaitanya accused of breaking?
qa.a: The class globe.

qa.q: What was Chaitanya feeling in the corridor?
qa.a: Angry, with his chest burning; he wanted to kick the door and shout.

qa.q: What did Chaitanya do the next morning that worked better than shouting?
qa.a: He calmly asked to explain, said the globe was already cracked, and named Veena as a witness.

qa.q: How might Chandrika Ma'am feel when Chaitanya comes calmly the next day?
qa.a: Willing to listen, and perhaps unsure about her quick judgment, since she agrees to ask Veena.

grounding: A boy wrongly blamed by a teacher feels hot anger, talks to his sister, and calmly explains the next day.

passage: In Class 5, our Hindi teacher once tore up my test because she thought I was whispering answers to Yamini. I'm Simran. I wasn't. Yamini had asked to borrow my eraser, and I had shaken my head. My face went hot, and my chest burned so hard I thought I'd explode. I wanted to shout, 'You never listen!' I almost did. Instead I sat on my hands until the bell, so angry my ears rang. After school I wrote down exactly what happened and read it to Papa. He said my anger made sense. The next day, calmer, I showed the teacher my note. Yamini said the same. The teacher gave me a new test paper. I was still angry that week, but I was glad I hadn't shouted.

qa.q: What had Yamini asked to borrow?
qa.a: Simran's eraser.

qa.q: What was Simran feeling when the test was torn up?
qa.a: Furious; Simran's face went hot and the burning in the chest felt ready to explode.

qa.q: How did Simran handle the anger wisely?
qa.a: By sitting on both hands instead of shouting, writing down what happened, reading it to Papa, then calmly showing the teacher the next day.

qa.q: How did Papa see Simran's anger?
qa.a: As making sense after being wrongly blamed.

grounding: A child wrongly blamed by a teacher feels burning anger but waits, then calmly explains what happened the next day.
